domains.title: Yongwang, the Dragon King
domains.subtitle: sovereign of the seas, storms, and waters
domains.lead: Yongwang is the dragon king, ruler of the seas and controller of rain, storms, and the waters upon which human life depends in Korean tradition. The name means "Dragon king" and belongs to the domain "Dragon King, Sea." Yongwang is the dragon king, a powerful deity of the sea who controls storms, rain, and the abundance of fish. He is worshipped especially in coastal fishing communities, where rituals ask for safe voyages and plentiful catches.

cards.name: Dragon King
cards.desc: Yongwang rules the seas as a royal dragon of immense power.

cards.name: Ruler of Seas
cards.desc: He governs tides, currents, and the creatures of the deep.

cards.name: Rain and Storms
cards.desc: The dragon king controls the weather that brings both life and destruction.

cards.name: Fisherfolk Protector
cards.desc: Coastal communities depend on Yongwang for safe voyages and abundant fish.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Yongwang is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Underwater Palace
myths.text: Yongwang is believed to live in a magnificent palace beneath the sea, where he keeps treasures, controls the tides, and commands armies of fish, turtles, and dragons. Fishermen who offended Yongwang risked storms and empty nets.

myths.title: The Yongwang-gut
myths.text: Coastal communities held Yongwang-gut, shamanic rituals dedicated to the dragon king. Offerings of rice, fruit, and specially prepared food were set afloat or presented on the shore to secure calm seas and abundant catches.

myths.title: The Visitor to the Dragon King
myths.text: Korean folktales sometimes tell of a poor but virtuous person who is carried to Yongwang's palace and rewarded with a magical gift. Such stories teach respect for the sea and warn against greed.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 龍 (yong, "dragon") and 王 (wang, "king"). Read 용왕 in Korean, it denotes the royal dragon sovereign of the waters, a figure shared across East Asian religions.

nameVariations.note: Alternate term for dragon spirit, especially in shamanic contexts.

originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Yongwang, the Hangul form is 용왕 and the Hanja form is 龍王. Hangul ‘용왕’ and Hanja ‘龍王’; the figure is shared with East Asian dragon-king traditions but has distinct Korean cultic forms. The ASCII form yongwang is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Yongwang is the scholarly citation form.
syncretism: Yongwang is part of a broader East Asian dragon-king tradition, with close parallels in Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese religion. In Korea the figure was absorbed into both Buddhism and shamanism, appearing as a donor or protector in Buddhist temples and as a sovereign spirit in gut rituals. Daoist cosmology supplied iconography and ritual methods for invoking rain. Despite these borrowings, the Korean Yongwang has a distinctive local colouring tied to fishing villages, coastal geography, and the hazards of the Korea Strait.
culturalLegacy: Yongwang remains a vivid figure in Korean coastal culture, appearing in temple art, village rituals, seafood markets, and popular media. Dragon king imagery decorates boats, restaurants, and festivals, and prayers for safe fishing continue in many communities. The figure also influences Korean environmental thought, serving as a symbol of the sea's power and the need for respectful relations with marine ecosystems. In games and animation, Yongwang often appears as a majestic dragon lord.
extendedMeditation: Yongwang invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
